4. At the trial prosecution examined 7 witnesses. RV:. 1 informant Sergeant Shahin Iqbal who proved F.I.R. Ext. 1 and seizure list. Ext. 2. He was cross-examined by the defence. P.W. 2 A.S.I. Salam who received F.I.R. filed by P.W. 1 filled up F.I.R. from Ext. 3 and started P.S. case. He was also cross-examined by defence. P.W. 3 Ayub Ali, P.W. 4 Md. Hazrat Ali, P.W. 5 Md. Delwar Hossain, P.W. 3, 4 and 5 were seizure list witness. P.W. 3 and 5 were declared hostile by prosecution but cross-examined by prosecution but not cross-examined by defence. P.W. 6 Md. Mohsin who was not cross-examined by defence. P.W. 7 1/0 Md. Fazlur Rahman who pre-pared Map with Index Ext. 4 and 5. During investigation he examined wit-nesses and recorded their statements under Section 161 of the Code and after closure of investigation he submitted charge sheet against accused Abu Baker Siddique under Section 19(Ka)(Cha) Arms Act, read with Special Powers Act, 1974. He was cross-examined by defence. After closure of prosecution evidence Abu Baker was examined under Section 342 of the Code and his statement was recorded. Defence adduced no evidence. Defence plea was of innocence and false implication. 

 5. Upon consideration of the evidence on record learned trial court found accused guilty for offence under Section 19A Arms Act the offence under Section 19(ka)(cha) of the Arms Act and accordingly convicted and sentenced him to suffer R.I. for 12 years and to pay fine of Tk. 2000/- in default to suffer R.I. for 3 months more vide judgment dated 24.7.96. 

 9. Learned Advocate in this regard refers two decisions reported in 5 B.L.C. page 248 and page 501 and submits that seizure and recovery of gun and curtiz from the accused was not according to provisions of Section 103 Cr.P.C. So the seizure and recovery of arms of the pre-sent case vide Ext. 2 cannot be acceptable in law. He submits that when P.W. 3, 4, 5 being seizure list witnesses did not sup-port the seizure and recovery of arms to have been made in their presence Ext. 2 (seizure list) can not be used against the appellant in as much as there being no other independent witness except P.W. 1, 2 and 3 including informant who all were police officials who were interested in the result of the case. In such regard he refers to the decision reported in 12 B.I,.D page 126 where in it was held that police wit-ness being interested in the result or the case should not be reliable. P.W. 6 Mahasin Sk. stated that he knew nothing about the occurrence. He shows that if the evidence of P.W. 3, 4, 5 and 6 be excluded from consideration and calculation there remains the only solitary evidence of informant P.W. 1 Sergeant Shahin lqbal who being informant of the case was likely to be interested in the result of the case. He shows that P.W. 2 A.S.I. A. Salam being duty officer of the thana received Or writ-ten. F:2-.R: from informant and started P.S. case and P.W. 7 was the 1/0 who submit-ted charge sheet after investigation. 

 10. Placing all above materials from the evidence on record learned Advocate submits that there being no legal evidence against the appellant he is entitled to get acquittal having found not guilty of the offence under Section 19(a)(f) of the Arms Act and should be directed to be set at liberty having allowed this appeal. 

 11. Learned A.A.G. appearing for the state respondent submits that there are some differences and anomalies between F.I.R. and evidence of informant as P.W. 1 at the trial as already agitated and pointed out by the learned Advocate for the appellants. He argues that there is nothing in evidence as to why the informant would file the false case against the appellant had the occurrence not been at all true. He submits that it was an occurrence during day time. Had it been false definitely there would have been reaction agitation among the people in the said Bazar area. But he frankly admits that there have been some differences and anomalies on some material facts as already shown on behalf of appellant. He finally contends that the appeal may be disposed of according to law as he cannot submit against evidence on records. 

 12. It appears that the charge against the convict appellant was for offence under Section 19(a)(0 of Arms Act for recovery of arms and ammunition like shutter gun and 2 live curtiz from his possession. Learned trial court found the convict appellant guilty under Section 19A Arms Act for recovery of short gun and live curtiz from his possession. Menimum punishment of the above offence is not less than 10 years. So when the charge is grave, the evidence must also be very satisfactory convincing and unimpeachable. Learned trial court having found the appellant guilty under Section 19A Arms Act convicted and sentenced him to suffer R.I. for 12 years and also to pay fine of Tk. 2000/- in default to suffer R.I. for 2 months more. 

 15. Above difference, and anomalies between F.I.R. Ext. 1 and deposition of P.W. 1 as stated above cast reasonable doubt as to the truth of the prosecution story. P.W. 3, 4, 5 and 6 stated in their respective deposition that they did not go with informant to the thana when F.I.R. was lodged. P.W. 3, 4 and 5 as seizure list witnesses stated that they were not pre-sent when recovery and seizure of the gun and curtiz were made. Rather they stated that only L.T.I. of P.W. 3 and signatures of P.W. 4 and 5 were taken on the seizure list by the police. So seizure and recovery of the arms and ammunition (Mat. Ext. 1 and II) from the actual possession and control of accused Abu Baker Siddique was not proved beyond all reasonable doubt. So the decision in the case of Juel V.S. State and Harun Bepary Vs. State reported in 5 B.L.C. page 248 and page 501 as cited on behalf of the appellant are found applicable in the present case in as much as seizure and recovery must be made in compliance of the provisions of Section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It appears that the provision of the said Section 103 of the Code were not duly complied in case of seizure and recovery of the arms and amunition vide Ext. 2. 

 16. It is true that nothing is in evidence whether the informant had any previous grudge or enemity with the accused. But law required that in order to find the accused guilty under Section 19A of the Arms Act read with Special Powers Act. 1974 wherein minimum punishment is not less than 10 years for seizure and recovery of arms and ammunition from the possession and control of the accused there must be unimpeachable and safely reliable evidence on the record. From our above scrutiny it transpires that seizure and recovery of Mat Ext. 1 and II in presence of P.W. 3, 4 and 5 Ayub Ali, Hazrat Ali and Delwar Hossain was not proved beyond doubt. Besides them there remains only the sole evidence of informant P.W. 1 Sergeant Shahin Iqbal whose evidence is also not unimpeachable for the reasons as already noticed above. P.W. 2 and 7 are police officers including I/O and they are formal witness only. P.W. 1, 2, 7 being police officers were interested in the result of the case cannot be considered to be impartial and independent witnesses to be reliable. In such connection reliance was put on the decision in the case of Mati Miah V.S. State reported in 12 B.L.D. page 126 wherein it was held that police persons being interested in the result of the case can be trusted as impartial witness in the absence of any independent witness in the case. Above decision finds application in the instant case also. 

 17. Having considered facts, circumstances and evidence on record we are of the view that required story satisfactory and unimpeachable evidence having not available in the case against the appellant trial court had no legal evidence before it to find appellant guilty under Section 19A Arms Act read with Special Powers Act. 1974 to convict and sentence the appellant vide impugned judgment dated 24.7.96 which accordingly calls for interference by this Court.
